I 'had shown by information that I had received from a local creamery in my constituency that the price of butter had been reduced four cents a pound this spring owing to the competition of Australian butter. I obtained from the Bureau of Statistics the importations of butter

into Canada for the period from October 1,
1924	to March 31, 1925 and from October 1,
1925	to March 31, 1926. I book those periods because the trade treaty with Australia came into effect on October 1, 1925. The following are the importations of butter for those periods:

When we compare these respective periods, therefore, we find that whereas we have imported from Australia and New Zealand butter to the total value of $1,839,159 during the time the treaty has been in effect, our imports amounted on the other hand only to the sum of $833 when there was no treaty. During the month of March of this year I happened to see in a window of one of the retail produce concerns in the city of Ottawa ,a display of Australian butter. I went in and made certain inquiries and learned that at that time this particular concern was selling between 300 and 400 pounds of dairy butter per week, and not only had they at that time no local butter in stock but for the three weeks prior to that they had not sold one pound of the Canadian product. And that store was only one of a chain of some fourteen shops owned by that concern. At the same time the three prairie provinces were exporting dairy butter as western Canada has overtaken production and is on an export basis twelve months in the year. I do not see why any government should subject the producers of butter in western Canada to such competition. They have to export their butter over thousands of miles of railway and then across the Atlantic to the markets of Great Britain while the people of Ontario cities are purchasing butter produced in Australia.
I want to deal for a few minutes now with the situation as it has developed in the province of Manitoba. Until now Manitoba has been almost entirely an agricultural province, but we shall not always remain a purely farming community. As a matter of fact the change is taking place to-day. Three-fifths of the land area of Manitoba is unsuitable for agricultural development. Up to the present we have depended entirely upon the growing of grain, but to-day the people of the province are beginning to realize the importance of development along other lines. There is now being built in Manitoba at Fort Alexander a pulp mill which, when

completed, will have an output of 100 tons of pulp per day. During the last session of the legislature railway bonds to the extent of $3,500,000 were guaranteed by the provincial government for the building of a railway from Mile 8 on the Hudson Bay line to the Flin Flon mine, the guarantee to become effective only when the Flin Flon people expend thirteen or fourteen million dollars on development work in that area. The legislature has also guaranteed bonds for a railway from Winnipeg into the Bice lake mining area. The people of the province are coming more and more to appreciate the importance of general development along various industrial lines. The province, as I have said before, will not always depend solely upon one industry, the growing of grain. To become prosperous we mugt not only diversify our farming but we must branch out into other industrial activities. We have in Manitoba a water power capable of very considerable development. Indeed, competent engineers have expressed the opinion that there is as much potential hydro electric power available on the Nelson river, flowing into Hudson bay, as has been developed on the Niagara, and wre have in Winnipeg the cheapest hydro-electric power to be found on the American continent.
With the resources latent in the province of Manitoba, including pulpwood and minerals, and with the electrical power available there is no reason why our province should not become one of the greatest manufacturing centres of this Dominion. We can manufacture in Winnipeg and in Manitoba generally, we should manufacture the agricultural implements needed in the province and other parts of the west and we have also the facilities for manufacturing our own boots and shoes, our own clothing and other necessities. It is because the people of the province have wakened to the necessity for general industrial development that, in my opinion, there are in this House seven Conservative members from Manitoba whereas in the last parliament there were none. The development of the province along one line is not in the best interests of the people of Manitoba any more than it would be in the interests of the Dominion as a whole if the activities of the people were centred in one industry. A few years ago we bent our efforts to the development of one industry, namely, the growing of grain and as a result of that one-sided development the people of the province suffered whenever there happened to be a poor crop. The greatest handicap under which we have suffered in

The Budget-Mr. Murphy
the past, and from which as a matter of fact we are suffering to-day, has been that restricted policy which has been the means of driving hundreds and thousands of our young men away from the province. Many of the sons of our farmers in Manitoba, on reaching the age of discretion, decided that they did not want to become farmers. Some of them entered the learned professions and some of them took advantage of the technical school in Winnipeg to fit themselves for an engineering career. With what result? When they had received their education and had graduated they found that there was no opportunity for them to apply their talents in their own country. From my own town of Neepawa many young men, after obtaining scholarships in our educational institutions, have drifted away. I do not know of one of those young men who . took the engineering course in Manitoba who is to-day in employment in Canada. They have all migrated to the United States. I am sure the same is true of other parts of the province.
Not only do we need the establishment and development of new industries in Manitoba, but we require also, for the greatest success, the completion of the Hudson Bay railway. I do not intend to deal at any length with this subject nor, to dwell upon the circumstances whereby this road has been left in its incomplete state, having been built within ninety miles or so of its terminus. Every government, leader and parliament since 1881 have committed themselves to the building of this road. In 1881 charters were granted by the government of Sir John A Macdonald to two companies for the undertaking and in 1884 the same government made a land grant of 6,400 acres per mile in Manitoba and 12,800 acres per mile in what was then the Northwest Territories, to insure the building of the Hudson Bay railway. As a result of that policy the road was built up to the present site of the town of the Pas.
I was interested in reading in the Ottawa Journal of May 11 of the present year, an editorial on the Hudson Bay railway. I shall not read the whole of the article, but I shall quote certain facts which the writer thought he had deduced from a debate which had taken place in the Senate this year:
Fact No. One: That lands sold in the west under the legislation of 1908 had no relation whatever to the construction of the Hudson Bay railway.
Fact No. Two: That these lands would have been sold had the Hudson Bay railway never been mentioned.
Fact No. Three: That none of the lands sold was in the Hudson bay area.
Fact No. Four: That, consequently, the whole of the $21,000,000 thus far spent upon the Hudson Bay railway has come out of ordinary national revenue, i.e. the taxpayer of the country.
At this point I should like to pay a compliment to the two daily papers published in the city of Ottawa. I have read them very carefully ever since my arrival in the capital in January, and I really think they are two very high class journals, but on the subject of the Hudson Bay railway the Ottawa Journal seems to suffer from a kind of mental hydrophobia. About the year 1896 or 1897, Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, a firm of railway contractors, undertook to build a railway from Gladstone, Manitoba, to Dauphin. At the same time they purchased from Mr. Sutherland who had obtained a charter in 1881 for the building of the Hudson bay road, a controlling interest in the South Saskatchewan and Hudson Bay Railway Company. When the line was built as far as Winnipegosis, Mackenzie & Mann continued westerly into the province of Saskatchewan rather than on to Hudson bay. In 1905, upon the creation of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, the demand became insistent for the completion of the Hudson Bay road. And the Hon. Frank Oliver, the then Minister of the Interior, on behalf of the government entered into an agreement with Mackenzie & Mann under the terms of which they relinquished the Hudson Bay charter and undertook to build a line from a point on the Dauphin and Prince Albert line to the Saskatchewan river, the government undertaking to sell sufficient homestead and preemption lands to provide for the completion of the road to the bay. As a result of that policy Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann built from a point on the Dauphin and Prince Albert line to the site of the present town of The Pas.
I have said that the government of the day entered into a contract with Mackenzie & Mann in 1905 by which the firm relinquished their charter. In 1908 the federal government caused an amendment to the Dominion Lands Act to be passed. On that occasion Hon. Frank Oliver said he found incongruities in the act which made the administration difficult. He also stated, as one reason why he wanted these amendments made to the act, that it was not the policy of the Laurier government to make grants of land towards the building of railways. In that connection I would refer to the debates of 1908, ag reported in volume 6 of Hansard. At page 11130 of that volume I find Mr. Oliver reported as saying:
Therefore, it is a plain proposition. There is, as it were, a (mortgage standing against the lands of the
The Budget-Mr. Murphy

northwest in respect to aid to a railway to Hudson bay. The necessity of such an outlet is greater than ever before and is more impressed on the minds of the people than ever before. Therefore in wiping out the mortgage upon the lands on behalf of a railway to Hudson bay, if we undertook to do as we propose in this act, it is necessary that we should place something in its stead, and that is the proposition that I desire to lay before the House.
Then further on the the same page:
That is to say, in regard to certain sections to allow the 'homesteader to buy an adjoining quarter section at a fixed price under settlement conditions. We believed that by the revival of this privilege we would create a new source of revenue to the Dominion treasury that would be adequate to meet the responsibilities which would have to be assumed by the construction of a railway to the bay.
And again, on page 11135, he is reported as saying:
There was no suggestion of restriction of the area to which the bill of last year applied.
Mr. Oliver had introduced amendments the year before but they had not been adopted; they were dropped.
My if ear was that a question might have been raised as to whether the provision /was adequate or not. What I had in view was to place before parliament a proposition that should put beyond question the fact that we bad adequately provided assistance from an entirely new source of revenue to enable the Hudson Bay railway to be built.
And again on page 11138:
The point we have din view in regard to this preemption matter is that there shall be a railway built to Hudson bay. If we can get a railway built to Hudson bay without any pre-emption provision at all then I am not insisting upon the pre-emption provision. But I am insisting upon the pre-emption provision as a means of ensuring the early building of a railway to Hudson bay.
And again at page 11150, in answer to a question, Mr. Oliver said:
We do not propose that the building of the railway Shall await ithe sale of 5,000,000 acres of this land, but we want to be able to say to the people of the country that if we find it necessary to pledge the credit of the country to an extent to raise sufficient money to aid in the building of the Hudson Bay railway, here is a new source of revenue that will relieve them of the burden of the responsibility they thus undertake.
I think, Mr. Speaker, from the evidence I have submitted, that the statements of the Ottawa Journal in the editorial in question are not facts but fiction. Now, from the year 1908 onward successive governments have recognized that the moneys derived from the sale of these lands were to be expended for the completion of the Hudson Bay road. The people of the west purchased lands on that definite understanding, and to-day there is a contractual obligation resting on the federal government to keep faith with these purchasers.

In answer to certain questions which I put on the order paper earlier in the session I obtained information to the following effect. Under the provisions of the act of 1908, as amended, there were 14,085,880 acres sold, of a value of approximately $42,257,640. Of that amount $19,837,288 have been collected, and there is still owing the sum of $7,300,000. leaving a total to the credit of the fund of $27,137,288. Of that amount $14,944,870 was expended up to February 28 of the present year, so that there is still a sum of $12,192,418 to the credit of the fund. I have said that the total amount collected was $19,837,288. Of this amount the sum of $14,944,870 has been spent,. leaving a cash credit ol $4,892,418. From the very first there has been determined opposition in certain quarters to the completion of the road and now that the completion is likely to be carried out, the opponents of the project are trying to reopen the question of the relative merits of Churchill and Nelson as a terminal. The port of Nelson was chosen as the terminal by two successive governments, after full investigation and report by competent engineers. Over $6,000,000 has been spent on the development of Port Nelson up to the present, and knowing these facts supporters of the road realize that a red herring is being drawn across the trail. But Mr. Speaker, we refuse to be drawn aside; we think there have been enough investigations during the last forty years, and that the time for action has now arrived.
The Conservative members from the wesi are frequently slightingly spoken of in this House as representing minorities. For the three prairie provinces, which may be taken as an economic unit, I would like to submit that the Conservative members do not represent minorities. I find that in these provinces during the last election there were oast for Conservative candidates 171,263 votes; for the Liberals 161,114 and for the Progressives 159,042. To elect each of the ten Conservatives from the prairie provinces it took 17,126 votes; for each Liberal 8,056, and for each Progressive 7,229. If the Conservatives were represented in this House according to the number of votes cast we would have at least twenty me-mbers instead of the ten we now have. I speak of this, Mr. 'Speaker, for the simple reason that the Progressives arrogate unto themselves the right to voice in this House the sentiments of the west, and I claim that the twenty-two Progressives, who represent only 116,114 votes do not express the feelings of the people of the prairie provinces any more than do the ten Conservatives, representing 171,263 votes.

The Progressive movement is not as strong and flourishing as it was a few short years ago. There is published in the west a paper called the Grain Growers' Guide, sometimes known as the Progressives' Bible. During some preceding years the subscription price has been $2 a year, $1 of which went to pay for the paper, the other dollar being the membership fee in the farmers' local. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make my position clear regarding the fiscal policy of the Conservative party. As I understand it the aim of the Conservative fiscal policy is to manufacture Canadian raw .products in Canada; to stimulate the development of Canadian resources by the Canadian people; to develop industries of the right nature; a policy which will provide employment for Canadian workmen and provide traffic for our railways; a policy which will keep Canadians in Canada and attract other people to our shores; a policy which will accomplish all these results without exploitation of the people and which will restore confidence by placing our tariff on an adequate, scientific, and above all a stable basis. If Canada is always to remain a country of magnificent distances with a sparse population fringing its borders; a nation of producers of primary products, then the policy which aims at free trade is the right one.
But I believe Canada has a greater destiny before her, and that the proper way to make our country as far as possible a self-sufficient nation is lay means of a national protective policy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider it my duty
to take part in the debate which has been going on in this House for several days concerning what we have agreed to call the budget.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in joining my congratulations to those, most flattering and most sincere, which you have already received since the beginning of the session, on the great honour which has come to you and of which we are all proud.
You will find it quite natural for a beginner to crave your indulgence should my inexperience cause me to commit some faux pas, which will undoubtedly happen despite my best efforts to prevent it. Not having the advantage of sufficient fluency in the English tongue to permit of my speaking here the language of the very great majority of the members of this parliament, I do not feel called upon, however, to make excuses, since both languages are official and since I am convinced moreover, being true to my race, of the rights and the beauties of the tongue I speak. Allow me, in passing, to congratulate most sincerely the hon. member for Northeast Toronto (Mr. Baker) on the splendid example he gave his fellow countrymen, and mine, the other day, when he spoke French in this House.	.
I have no intention, Mr. Speaker, of discussing in detail the Speech from the Throne, nor, especially, the very able and very sincere budget speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on April 15th. I merely wish to offer a few comments on certain questions which may interest the voters of my riding as also the voters of the district where I have the pleasure and the advantage of residing. Following the example set by several speakers since the opening of the session I take pleasure in acquainting you a little with the feelings and the needs of my constituents.
I shall not hide from you, Mr. Speaker, that the voters of the county of Lotbiniere, which I have the honour to represent in this House, are very well pleased with the economic situation this government has placed them in. I represent a farming district where industries are few and far between. In certain parishes of course one will find small industrial establishments due to the initiative and energy of enterprising individuals; these
The Budget-Mr. Verville

establishments deserve to survive, and deserve all the encouragement the federal government can give them. But those who are at the head of them are workers who do not rely solely on legislation and tariff increases to succeed in business; but who rely chiefly on their own initiative and on the industry of their workmen.
As regards the farmers, who make up the large majority in the constituency I represent, they have felt, and still feel, the terrible crisis which followed the war. They are the ones who need protection, but that kind of protection which, while favouring them, will work no harm to the other classes of the community. To my mind the best protection the present administration could offer the agricultural class would be to afford them easier access to the markets of the world for the sale of their produce. Our farmers do not fear competition; they would rather have access to the markets than keep their produce at home so as to avoid competition.
When the election was being fought last fall I had the advantage,-if it might be called an advantage-of being present at a large Conservative rally; and it amused me to hear distinguished speakers, with magnificent voice and gesture, their arms spread as though on a cross, their eyes lifted skywards, tell us that things looked very dark in the homes of our farmers, that even bread was getting scarce and that those who wished to avoid death by starvation had no choice but to nail boards over the windows of their homes and to leave Canada for the States. And the Liberal party was held responsible for all this. The result of the election shows that our good farmers are intelligent enough to judge their situation for themselves and that they laugh at calamity howlers just like the citizens of the province of Quebec laughed at Mr. Patenaude. At all events the situation of the farmers in my county, and I have reason to believe that the same thing is true elsewhere, has improved considerably within the last few years. And I claim that this is due in great measure to the wise administration of the present government during the last five years. One is inclined to wonder if Providence is not on the side of the Liberal party for whenever that party takes over the administration of public affairs conditions improve and the country prospers; while the facts prove that exactly the opposite happens each time the Conservative party is at the helm. I am loath to acquire a reputation as an overzealous partisan for speaking thus frankly; but I have always said what I thought and I do not wish to lose this habit

in the House. Besides, the facts are there to prove the truth of what I say; and if we discard the red or blue cloths which blindfold us we must admit that these things are true. At any rate the voters I have had the pleasure ^ of meeting since the beginning of the session are pleased with the present government and congratulate the Liberal party for having stayed in power and thus ensured the prosperity of the country. Since the Finance Minister brought down his budget the people have been rejoicing; my constituents, like everybody else, have expressed their deep satisfaction at all the good financial tidings contained in the budget speech.
The government is surely deserving of our most hearty congratulations for their excellent work and the marvels accomplished. After five years of administration, having found public affairs in a terrible mess, confronted with the complete disorganization which followed the war, and despite the acute crisis which has been felt for several years, the government is able to announce to the country a not inconsiderable surplus and moreover its determination to lift some $25,000,000 of taxes off the shoulders of the Canadian taxpayer. I fully appreciate that there is no putting an end to politics; nevertheless one must recognize facts and call things by their right names. For my part, and I believe I speak for the great majority of my constituents, the present government deserves our congratulations for all the excellent measures they have brought to our attention and I consider it a duty to offer them mine.
Since the opening of the session it has been essential that we should discuss each day and every day Maritime rights, western rights, and the rights of other provinces. You will bear witness, Mr. Speaker, that we have not tired the House with the question of the rights of the province of Quebec. I would not wish to revive the old problem of provincial rights; and if I mention the matter it is merely because I wish to explain my own attitude; I believe in giving to each province, as to the representatives of every county, the greatest possible measure of justice, with absolute impartiality, but with firmness. I understand that certain needs are felt in each riding, and I shall tell you nothing new when I say that Lotbiniere county has needs of its own. There is one problem in particular which interests my county and the neighbouring counties on the south shore.
Since 1922 my predecessor in this House has striven to have a proper roadway afforded to vehicular traffic on the Quebec bridge.

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
A detailed report on this question must have been forwarded to the hon. Minister of Railways.
Let me draw your attention to the following fact:	Resolutions asking for the construction of a road for vehicles on the Quebec bridge were adopted by the county councils of Lotbiniere and Levis and the municipal councils of almost every parish of my riding and addressed to the Department of Railways and Canals. Owing to the enormous and ever-increasing traffic of visitors in that part of the province, in summer, and to the very important traffic of the people of my riding and of the two adjacent counties and the city of Quebec, the construction of that road for vehicles on the Quebec bridge is now a necessity. The present government would indeed earn the gratitude of the voters of Lotbiniere were they to start work on this improvement without delay. A minute ago, I said that this improvement is now a necessity and I will add that an inquiry that was conducted has proven the idea to be a practical one. The engineers of the National railways are of the opinion, I am told, that there is in the centre of the bridge plenty of room for the construction of such a road and that the approaches and the floor of the bridge could be so arranged as in no way to interfere with the railways. As you know, in recent years, commissions have been flourishing and if I had my way, I would follow the suggestion that was made before and I would appoint a commission that we could call "the Quebec bridge highway commission." which would be authorized to undertake the work for the project I am putting before the House now. It will be said, I suppose, by certain parties, that at a time when the government are trying to balance the budget, it would not be fair to undertake such a work that may necessitate a large expenditure. I may answer that the country is well able to spend to-day half a million dollars which is the amount required for this work. I will say more: I believe that the Federal government could easily come to an understanding with the provincial government and the Quebec city council and share with those two bodies the cost of the enterprise.
I respectfully submit those facts to the government and hope that they will give them their best attention. There cannot be any [DOT] politics or patronage in connection with the building of this road, its construction is in the public interest and is a public utility; everybody would profit by the road and be glad to have it.
Before I take my seat, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Seguin) for the good move he made last week when he insisted on the use of bilingual postage stamps. I wholly agree with him and I am glad to see that there are yet in this House well advised people who wish to preserve for the province of Quebec and its inhabitants of French descent their full rights. Let us hope, Mr. Speaker, that we will always remember in all the measures that come before the House, as in the different departments of the government, that in the province of Quebec French Canadian citizens have rights equal to those of the citizens of the Maritime provinces, or of the prairie provinces or any other provinces as well and 'that those Quebec citizens are always respectful of the rights of others in the different parts of the country, but do not want others to abuse their generosity; they want others to remember that in this country the French Canadians are the pioneers unwilling to trespass on the rights of others and at the same time intent on safeguarding their own rights.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr
Speaker, at this stage of the budget debate it is appropriate that addresses should be as short and as pointed as circumstances will permit. I therefore propose to take a very brief portion of the time of the House this afternoon in dealing with some of the matters that are presented by the budget. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Verville) will pardon me if I do not deal directly with his address. I shall have to await the translation of it, but I assure him that I shall do him the honour to read it when the translation is available. It did not sound to me like the speech of a free trader, and I am going to assume that, like many of the other representatives of his province, he is a protectionist, and perhaps therefore we have very much -in common and there would not be very much to criticize in his speech.
There have been, Mr. Speaker, several descriptions of this budget. It has been described as a popular budget. No doubt it was intended to be such, but popularity is as a rule of short life, particularly in matters political, and this budget is not, I think, as popular as it was on the day on which it was delivered. It has also been called the people's budget. I remember in connection with one budget-I think it was the first one delivered by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb)-one hon. member of this House described it as a juggler's budget. That wa3 because of the fact that the figures were rather difficult to understand, rather difficult to analyze, and perhaps did not really disclose clearly the actual state of affairs. I think it

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
was an appropriate description of that particular budget. I would describe this budget as one of insincerity and inconsistency. I say insincere, because of the manner in which the tax reductions in this budget are mentioned and dealt with. A great deal of credit is claimed for a reduction of taxation, and we are always pleased to note anything of that character, but M|r. Speaker, I think it would only have been fair and proper for the Finance Minister to point out that several of these taxes that have been reduced by this government were first put on by this government, and others that have been reduced were increased by this government.
Then in connection with the income tax reduction, which is, as I have said, very welcome, it comes only about two years too late. On this side of the House we have been pressing for it for the la^t two or three years, in pointing out the disparity between the taxation in Canada and the taxation in the United States, much to the disadvantage of Canada, in respect of its capital and of its industry.
The sales tax was, as hon. members know, increased by this government from 3 to 6 per cent, and subsequently reduced to 5 per cent. The stamp tax on cheques was very materially increased by this government, and remains as it was. An entirely new tax was put upon receipts. That has now been taken off, and is being claimed as an achievement.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that when all this is taken into consideration, no real or substantial credit is due to this government in connection with the reduction of taxation which was, in the first instance, imposed or increased by this government.
I say this budget is inconsistent because it violates the clear, definite, positive pledges given by this government prior to the last election, and subsequent to it in the Speech from the Throne, in which it was stated definitely that tariff changes would be the subject of investigation by an expert commission before any reductions were made. The reduction in income tax gives rise to some speculation or comment as to the attitude of our Progressive friends. In the last parliament they were strongly in favour of this tax and loud in their protestations against any reduction in it. We have not heard in this debate one word of criticism from that section of the House in connection with the reduction in the income tax, and we wonder why this is the case. We wonder if a trade has been made, and if they have withheld criticism from the reduction in the income tax because of the concessions they are getting in respect of the reduction in taxation

on automobiles. It is a matter for speculation, a matter for fair inference. Possibly before the debate is closed we may have some explanation of it.
While there is a reduction of taxation in this budget, there is no considerable relief for business nor any real stimulus to industry. What is vitally needed is a sweeping reduction of sales taxes and of super taxes on income in order that capital may be set free for the expansion of industrial enterprises and for projects of national development. As necessary is a revision of the tariff that will check destructive American competition with Canadian farm and factory products, give greater security to certain industries affected by the British preference, and guard against the inflow of goods made by cheaper labour in some of the countries of Europe.
The truth is that the greater burdens laid upon capital and industry in Canada as compared with the United States almost equal any protectionist duties levied in the interest of home industries, while the goods and products of Canada are shut out of the neighbouring country by a tariff which shows no mercy for Canadian farmers or manufacturers. It is even doubtful if the heavy Canadian surtaxes bring in as much revenue as would be realized under lower schedules. Taxes designed to punish the rich always bear more heavily upon the poor, and nothing is so fatal as scarcity of capital in an undeveloped country and particularly in a country lying, as we do alongside a rich and powerful neighbour with industries equipped and capital organized to challenge the commercial ascendancy of all other nations.
The new income-tax rates fixed by the budget give a measure of needed relief to smaller income-tax payers, but the schedules lack the essential element of equity; and when the best is said for what Mr. Robb has done, his budget is not so much a "people's budget" as a politicians' budget, designed to make votes for the government rather than to give fair play to capital, infuse energy into business, increase prosperity, and accelerate national progress.
The tariff policy of this country has been a subject of discussion for many years, and we had thought that it was fairly well established that a reasonable measure of protection was the policy of all parties until this government came into power. Certainly this is a matter which should be settled and established at the earliest possible moment. We hear voices in this parliament in favour of free trade and we are looking to the time when this issue will come before the people, clean and clear-cut, when it will not be en-

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
tangled with any side issue, and when it does come, Mr. Speaker, we, on this side of .the House have no doubt what the result will be. As I have said, we hear several voices, more in this House than in the last parliament, in favour of free trade and one may hope the matter may be forced to an issue at an early date. As to the policy of the leader of this party and those who support him in this House, there is absolutely no question whatever. We stand for a fair, reasonable and proper measure of protection for agriculture, for industry and for labour, and the fact that we stood for this in the last parliament, went to the country with fifty-one followers, and came back with one hundred and sixteen is in itself sure proof that that policy met with the approval of a large portion of the electors. We have often been told of conditions in what is said to be free trade England, and it is interesting for us to note just exactly what is taking place there. 1 have here an extract which I think is worth reading, taken from the Saturday Evening Post of April 17, 1926. This is a very excellent American periodical and its editorial column is strong and clean. I think this article may be looked upon as a fair pronouncement and a fair indication of an independent opinion with regard to what is taking place in England. The article is entitled "Protection in Great Britain" and reads:
The gradual trend to a protective tariff in Great Britain is in some respects the most notable of the postwar developments in economic policy. Protection has come into Great Britain through the back door of safeguarding the industries, but it has made entrance just the same. Each industry must pro/e its case, but apparently the appeal is made to a sympathetic bench. The debates in parliament and the controversies in the public press are illuminating and sometimes astounding. The protestant language employed by free traders is sometimes unrestrained to the point of insult. When so highly developed a British industry as cutlery seeks and obtains a high protective tariff, it is time to sit up and take notice, for something unusual is going on.
Taking cutlery as an illustration, the British goods are not only losing out in foreign markets but the foreign goods are invading the home market. Confessedly less durable than the British goods, the invading foreign goods look as good and sell for less. Is this high price of British goods due to low productivity or overorganized labour? Is it the result of antiquated equipment and methods? Is it the consequence of poor entenprise? These are all suggested as explanations, and indignantly repudiated by the classes concerned. Is it the result of underpaid labour in the countries from which the cheap competing goods come? Is it the result of depreciated currences in competing countries?. Is the Dawes plan responsible? Or debt payments? These are all offered in explanation. Finally, quite a large group hold the gold standard responsible at once for the loss of foreign markets and for the invasion of the home market by cheap foreign goods. And, of course, the successfully competing
countries, ourselves included, flatter themselves that they have achieved a technical superiority over the British.
It is too early <m the process to determine the trutl*. Time would make the 'facts clear if the course of events were to continue undisturbed. But political action will intervene. The Liberal party has been the party of free trade. The Liberal party is breaking up. The two-party system will persist in Great Britain, but the two parties will be the Conservative and the Labour parties. The left wing of the Liberal party will go over to Labour, the right wing will join the Conservatives. A few outstanding figures among the Liberals will stand aloof, faithful to their creed and protestant without avail. Both the Conservative and the Labour 'parties lean toward protection, but for different reasons.

speechtext: What is the hon. member quoting from?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am quoting
from the Saturday Evening Post, April 17, 1926. The article continues:
With the dissolution of the Liberal party, free trade will pass into history. The doctrine of protection will take on an imperial complexion. There will be empire preferences, with higher duties against the outside world. It will be a strange sight to see the British Empire, whose foreign investments and positive balance of international trade rest on .free trade, undertake to deal as of old in her capacity of banker and shipper for other trading countries while setting up tariff duties at the briny borders of the United Kingdom. In the view of the traditional Liberal, it will be protection for senile, not for infant industries. In the view of the protectionists, it is an inevitable adaptation to a fundamentally changed world condition.
In that article there is food for thought on the part of those who favour protection and those who favour free trade. Whatever our views may be on this question I think we are all agreed that as far as possible we should have stability of tariff; that business should not be frequently disturbed by radical changes, by increases or reductions in the tariff. That I think is a fair statement and one that will find general assent. [DOT]
I have before me a statement made by the ex-Minister of Finance, the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding on this point. When he was delivering his budget speech in 1923 in this House, he said:
There is a thought which does not receive as much consideration as J. think sometimes it should be given in public discussion, and that is the desirability of something like tariff stability. Business men do not like
to be always threatened with changes in the tariff-
The tariff as it will be when the changes proposed today come into effect will be a moderate tariff and probably as low as the country can afford to have under present conditions. Of course we cannot expect that it will be satisfactory to everybody. It will not meet the desires of those who would rigidly apply the principles of free trade. It will not meet the wishes of the advocates of high protection.
The leader of the opposition at this point interjected:
It comes pretty close to it.

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
Mr. Fielding continued:
I think the country should be content to accept the tariff as it will now stand as one as fair and reasonable as can be prepared under all the circumstances, and business men should be able to carry on the various enterprises without the fear of being soon disturbed by further changes.
The very next session there was unfortunately for industry in this country a cut in several items of the tariff. I refer to the tariff on agricultural implements and the result to the allied industries has been very harmful. It is true that the larger industries-

To what class
and to what body of people has the reduction been harmful?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

To the smaller
factories that supply the parts to manufacturers of agricultural implements. I would call my hon. friend's attention to the fact that there has been a continued exodus of the workers of Canada to the United States. Many that I know personally have gone as a result of some of the factories not being able to continue to operate and to give them employment.

My hon. friend

I wonder how
long my hon. friend thinks Canada can stand an exodus at the rate at which it went on for a few years.

At a reduced
rate.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I say the
exodus cannot continue in such large numbers every year. Between five and six hundred thousand people have gone and more are going as a result of the recent changes and the threatened changes in the tariff. I

am sure my hon. friend will agree with the argument I am endeavouring to make that we should have reasonable tariff stability in this country. I do not like to quote at too great length, but for the benefit of the Minister of Public Works I will read this article that appeared in the Toronto Globe on Saturday, May 1, of this year, dealing with the question of tariff stability:
With his usual pointedness President Beatty of the Canadian Pacific Railway 'told the members of the Canadian Daily Newspapers' Association on Thursday night that what this country needed more than anything else was stability of tariff. It is a statement with which all business men will agree, regardless of their preference for high or low protection. As Mr. Beatty says, it is common sense, not politics.
Business has become so intricate, the elements entering into it so finely adjusted, that it is highly sensitive, and may be greatly affected by s'light changes in tariff. It is essential in a well-managed business that department costs bear a fixed relation to one another and to the complete product, while highspeed efficiency requires a minimum of lost motion in every avenue of expense and of waste material in every commodity used. It is plain that under these conditions it takes some time to establish basic costs upon which the machinery, both physical and human, will run with uninterrupted smoothness, and that uncertainty of obtaining and maintaining these conditions makes the life of a business rather precarious.
The tariff is not the only factor which may cause disturbance, but so long as an industry knows what contribution the tariff makes to raw material costs it is so much to the good in the matter of stability. It can commit itself to purchases on that basis, for a long time in advance if desirable. So President Beatty remarked that if he met a high-tariff man and a low-tariff man he would be disposed to say to them: "Gentlemen, fix it up bewteen yourselves, but fix it ami make it reasonably stable." He added the significant comment that important British and American companies in many lines of manufacture were waiting to invest money in this country, and would not come in until they knew what our tariff was to be for a reasonable length of time.
Periodical tariff "tinkering" has a disrupting effect on business. When changes are needed they should be made only after careful, scientific study, with due regard to the fiscal requirements of the country, but as infrequently as possible.
That is the point I was endeavouring to make and I would like the Minister of Public Works to consider it and the statements made in this paper which is friendly to his government.
That brings me to the question of the tariff on automobiles and the tariff reduction proposed by this budget. This subject of the reduction in the duty on automobiles has engaged the attention of this House on previous occasions and has been fully discussed. I would refer to Hansard of the session of 1925 when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) dealt with this matter, because his observations on that occasion are a little different from what he said in connection with the present budget. As reported on page 1185 of Hansard of 1925 the Minister

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
of Finance said, speaking of the amount of capital coming from the United States for investment in this industry:
If his statement ito-night is correct it would seem that there has been some Unlrted States capital invested in the business since then. But without going into that feature, I would remind the hon. gentleman that no matter where the capital comes from, the industry gives employment to Canadian labour. There are 78 plants engaged in the manufacture of automobiles and their accessories in Canada, employing Canadian labour, and subject (to Canadian taxation, a considerable amount im taxes finding its way into the Canadian treasury.
My hon. friend quoted some prices to show the difference in value between an automobile in the United States and one of similar pattern and style in Canada. I know of course that there is some discrimination, but we account for part of it ourselves. The hon. member will bear in mind that we place a sales tax on the automobile of 5 per cent, and we also impose a luxury tax of 5 per cent on automobiles costing up to $1,200. and 10 per cent on those over $1,200. I mention this figure to remind my hon. friend that the difference in the duty, even admitting his figures, does not account for the difference in the respective prices. I agree with the hon. gentleman that in many parts of Canada the automobile has become a necessity. But it as not always a necessity for there are many people owning and operating motor cars who in my
opinion would be better off without them	
As my hon. friend has truly said, we have in Canada a considerable number of cars. I do not remember the figures he gave but the record I have is 513,821. From the owners of these cars the provinces collect
in taxes the sum of $9,290,900.82	The fact
of the matter is that the automobile has cost the different provinces of Canada millions of dollars to improve their roadways besides huge sums annually to maintain them. I submit to the hon. gentleman that the automobile is a fair source from which to collect revenue.
That was in the session of 1925. At that time the Minister of Finance did not seem to be of the opinion that the duty should be *reduced.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If my hon. friend's party were returned to power would he recommend an increase in automobile duties?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my party is
returned to power, as I think it will be before very long, it will live up to the pledges it has given to the people. What we complain of is that this government has not honoured its pledges. It went to the Canadian people and said that, so far as the tariff was concerned, no changes would be made before there had been a careful and thorough investigation. That is exactly what should have taken place in connection with the industry I am now discussing, and that is the policy which my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) laid down in a resolution presented to this House in June last. It is the policy that will be carried out on our coming into power.
Now, I was dealing with the tariff reductions on automobiles. If it is desirable to reduce
the prices of automobiles-and I quite agree with the contention that as far as possible they should be reduced-the government had at its disposal a very sure and safe way of effecting sudh a reduction without injury to the industry. They could have removed the excise tax of five per cent on cars up to 81,200 and the sales tax on cars up to the same price. That would have meant a reduction in the case of a car costing $1,200 of $120 and it would have been a' very much greater reduction than will be secured through reducing the duties as now proposed. In the case of a car costing $2,000 there would be at once a difference in price of $200 if these two taxes were eliminated. Having made such a provision to secure reduced prices the government could then have conducted an investigation into the main industry and all its allied activities to ascertain just how much protection they were receiving. Had (they done so they would only have been following the course which they themselves outlined in their campaign speeches and in the Speech from the Throne.
This is the most severe and drastic cut in the history of the tariff as we have had it in Canada, and the effect will be far-reaching. Indeed, it is difficult to predict how serious the consequences will be, for there are so *many allied industries dependent upon the manufacture of automobiles dn .connection with the supplying of parts and materials, and from the standpoint of capital invested. The amount of capital invested is very large indeed. The automobile and allied industries embrace hundreds of manufacturers engaged in the development of raw materials in all stages up to the finished product, and over $100,000,000 of capital is invested. There are also vast numbers of workers involved. The budget in its direct and drastic tariff reduction has therefore created a state of tariff uncertainty which threatens to have far-reaching effects on the country's industrial development. Whatever may be the fate of industries which have been established in Canada behind the tariff protection which has now been removed, and some or all of Which industries may be closed as a result of imports from the United States, there can be little doubt that the establishment of further American plants in Canada, and the expansion of the industries already operating here, have been discouraged in a very definite way. The ramifications of the automobile industry can only be grasped when the extent of the purchases of manufacturers in the dhape of supplies and materials is taken into consideration. It is estimated that parts sold to motor manufacturers during the past year amounted to some $50,000,000. So that we
3364	COMMONS
The Budget-^-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
have, as I have said, a very severe and drastic cut in the tariff, made without investigation or proper consideration, and in violation of the pledges given by this government.
A very large deputation having waited upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and members of the cabinet in connection with this proposed reduction, the Prime Minister said that his government would be influenced not so much by numbers as by arguments. Apparently the voice of '3,000 people speaking as one had little weight with him, whereas the voice of a few members within this House seems to have had a great deal of influence. There is no doubt whatever that this reduction in the tariff, in the face of the pledge given by the government that there would be an investigation and in the face of the statement contained in the Speech from the Throne to the same effect, is a matter of political expediency, pure and simple, and has nothing whatever to commend it from any other source.
I wish to place on Hansard a resolution passed by the council of the town of Gananoque. There is no automobile factory in that town but there are several factories that supply parts required in the industry, and this resolution will reveal how far-reaching will be the effects of the proposed reduction. The resolution wras passed on April 20, 1926, and was forwarded to me in a letter addressed by the town clerk, Mr. J. H. Sampson. Mr. Sampson writes:
I am directed by the municipal council of the town of Gananoque to forward you the following resolution passed at their meeting last night:
That this council of the town of Gananoque views with regret and great alarm the prospect of serious injury to the automotive industry of Canada as a result of the federal government reducing the tariff of import duties on automobiles, and that, in view of the fact that the prosperity of the industries of this town depend so much upon the prosperity of the automobile industry of Canada, and that the prosperity of the town in general is so dependent upon the work which its factories offer, we feel justified in presenting this motion of formal protest at the action which the government has seen fit to take. To us it seems, beyond the possibility of doubt, that the industrial life of Gananoque is seriously threatened by the budget now before the federal House, and we do therefore present this protest, believing it will receive the consideration which it deserves, we do so further move that a copy be sent to the Prime Minister Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, as well as copies to the Hon. J. A. Robb and to our representative in the House of Commons, Mr. Hugh Alexander Stewart, K.C.
As I have said that shows how far-reaching the effect of a reduction in the tariff is. This deputation, it seems to me, furnished an unanswerable argument in connection with the proposed reduction. They referred to the paragraph in the Speech from the Throne dealing with tariff changes, and asked that
(.Mr. H. A. Stewart.]
there should be a thorough investigation before this reduction was put into effect. That is the position of these manufacturers, that is the position of these employees. I do not not know myself whether the duty is too high or too low, whether the proposed reduction is reasonable or unreasonable; all that I am contending for is that there should have been that thorough, complete, exhaustive, impartial investigation which the serious consequences of an action of this kind would warrant. It seems to me the action of the government in this matter is a breach of faith. Not only that, but it is a breach of contract, it is a breach of duty to Canadian industry and Canadian labour. The highest tribute that we can pay to an individual is to say of him that his word is his bond; and the highest tribute that could be paid to a government would be to say that it was honest, sincere and fearless in the discharge of its duties and fulfilment of its pledges. That tribute surely cannot be paid to this government by even its most ardent supporters. Rather must it be said that the making by them of a pledge is almost a sure indication that that pledge will be broken. We have had promises of tariff stability, but instead of tariff stability we have had tariff tinkering. We have had it to such an extent that the supporters of the government were compelled to rise in this House and register a protest. We have had it to such an extent that industry has become unsettled, it has lost confidence, there has been no expansion, and our people have been forced to go to the United States.
We had a pledge from this government, through its Prime Minister at Richmond Hill, that in view of the difficulties experienced in the last parliament, it would not attempt to carry on unless it was more strongly supported in the next; and although the result of that election was to defeat the Prime Minister and all of his ministers from Ontario, and to seriously reduce his following in the House, we find the government attempting to carry on in violation of the solemn pledge it gave to the people on that occasion. We had a pledge given to the House in the Speech from the Throne, a pledge which was very clear, definite and positive with repect to action in connection with the tariff. The House is very familiar with the government's pledge, but it will bear repeating. It reads as follows:
They believe that in the interest of industrial development every effort should be made to eliminate the element of uncrtainty with rspect to tariff changes; that changes in the tariff should be made only after the fullest examination of their bearing upon both primary and manufacturing industries, and that re-

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
presentations requesting increase or decrease of duties should be made the subject of the most careful investigation and report by a body possessing the necessary qualifications to advise the ministry with respect thereto. I do not see how any hon. member can vote against that amendment. It is an indictment that has not been and cannot b& answered. The pledge is there; the pledge comes from the government itself. The violation of it is there, and comes from the-government itself, and I cannot possibly see how any hon. member who desires to emphasize the necessity of candour and sincerity in public life can vote against this amendment.
I shall vote against this budget, Mr. Speaker, because it is a breach of faith; it is a breach of contract, and it is a breach of duty. The hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. Stewart) made a remark a few minutes ago, which I jotted down, to the effect that there has been no expansion in Canada. I am not going to answer that statement along the line of trying to defend any particular government of any particular party, but I shall answer it by quoting from an article that appears in the May number of Canadian Chemistry and Metallurgy. This article was written by an expert and concerns the pulp and paper industry in Canada. I shall quote only such portions as will serve to answer the remark made by my hon. friend who has just sat down. It says:
When one comes to survey the happenings in the pulp and paper industry during the last twelve months it is almost impossible to overcome a feeling of bewilderment at the number and magnitude of the projects which have been completed, which are under construction, or which have been planned and are about to be started. In practically all parts of Canada we hear of new mills being constructed and of established mills expanding, with the results that the industry is developing at an almost fantastic rate, which was absolutely undreamed of a couple of years ago, and which has no parallel in the paper making history of any other country in the world.
Of course, the great bulk of the paper produced is newsprint; and the expansion of this branch of the industry will best be visualized by quoting a few figures recently published by the Newsprint Service Bureau. During 1925 ten machines with a rated daily capacity of 890 tons were started up in Canada and Newfoundland (of which four machines with a capacity of 375 tons were in Newfoundland), while eighteen machines with a total rated capacity of 1,715 tons per day are scheduled to start up in 1928, only one of them being in Newfoundland. And the end is not yet in sight, for already work is well under way in connection with machines to be installed during 1927 and 1928.
It should be remembered, however, that the actual production of these machines may be, and probably will be, greater than the rated capacity. Competition has resulted in quite an appreciable reduction in the price of newsprint during the last two or three years, and the mills have been forced to increase operating efficiency so as to lower cost of production. Great strides have been made in this direction, and the good work which was begun a couple of years ago has been kept up and even improved upon, with very striking results. The Belgo mill at Shawinigan Falls, for instance, has a rated capacity of 390 tons, but has turned out up to 425 tons in 24 hours. In 1919 it was considered a good day's work at the Abitibi mill at Iroquois Falls, Ontario, when they turned out 240 tons a day; but recently the same machines produced 295 tons. This mill has since been enlarged to a rated capacity of 500 tons; the record production for a single day is very close to 550 tons, and the average daily production is in the neighbourhood of 525 tons.
When the members of the Progressive party toured the Maritime provinces just a year ago, we saw at the town of Edmundston on the St. John river a pulp mill being built on the Canadian side, and just across the river, on the American side, a paper mill was being built, and we came to the conclusion that 11011-214J
the two were owned by Americans, and that the idea was that the pulp mill on the Canadian side was being built to beat the embargo, and that the pulp would be run across the line and be manufactured into paper on the American side. The article goes on to say:
An interesting development has been what virtually amounts to the construction of a Canadian fine paper mill in the United States. The Fraser Companies had a large sulphite mill at Edmundston, New Brunswick. There was a ready market for their pulp in the United States; but if it were converted into paper in Canada ' it could not compete with American papers in the United States owing to the high customs duty imposed by the American tariff. As their pulp mill is on the international boundary, the company overcame tihe difficulty by building the paper mill at Madawaska, Maine, just across the river from their Edmundston mill. Not the least interesting feature of this combination is the big double pipe line through which the sulphite stock is pumped in slush form from the pulp mill on the Canadian side to the paper mill on the American side. The first machine of this two-machine mill was started up last November.
So Canadians are not only manufacturing their own paper supplies, but are invading the United States' market as well.
One other portion, of this article I should like to read because it concerns the Australian treaty, a treaty which the Progressive members of this House voted against a year ago because they thought it would be of no benefit to Canada, but which has proved Of benefit to Canada along lines not dreamed of one year ago. The article says:
But though newsprint throws other branches of the industry considerably in the shade, it must not be taken for granted that nothing is being done along other lines. The Australian trade treaty has already been of greater benefit to the Canadian paper industry than had been anticipated. It is now expected that Canada may obtain nearly half the Australian newsprint market, while the demand for Canadian book and writing papers is also good. Provincial Paper Company is developing its business in this promising market to good effect, and as a result has decided to go ahead with the installation of another machine in its Port Arthur mill. Another project directly traceable to the Australian treaty is the organization of the Canadian-Scottish Paper Mills, which will erect a coating mill for book and litho papers on the Pacific coast.
We have repeatedly heard it stated in this House since the opening of this session that if Canada is going to prosper, there will have to be quite a radical change in the tariff to look after the needs of Canadian industry, and that we must have what has been called tariff stability. Some have said that we should have a high tariff, and some newspapers have advocated a tariff, brick for brick, with the American tariff. Others proclaim that the policy of Canada from this time onwards must be a protectionist tariff, and Canada must be definitely committed to the policy of pro-

The evidence on this matter
is on record in the United States. I have not worked out the figures myself from the United States tariff. I have here a statement as to the effect of railway rates in the United States, and it reads as follows:
Railway rates are high because of high operating costs. So much of the income of the railroads is paid out for equipment, fuel, and wages, that all other expenditures are comparatively inconsiderable. The wages of two million railway men are unusually high prinoipaWy -because the cost of living is high beyond all precedent, and railway workers must be paid accord ingily. Fuel is high for the same reason-high wages in mine and transportation and high cost of retail distribution. Railway equipment ds extremely expensive, because of thigh, general wages, and because manufacturers of many products used in railway equipment are over-protected, and their prices are higher than they would be under a fair tariff. This affects 2,580,000 cars, 69,000 locomotives, rails and other supplies.
The cost of living to the people of the United States would be reduced about $3,000,000,000 by a moderate and reasonably protective -tariff dn lieu of the present Fordney law. This reduction in living costs would quickly bring a reduction dn freight charges, which reduction. Senator Capper, chairman o-f the Senate farm bloc, says is the most important matter before Congress in the interest of agriculture.
As transportation is an enormous charge upon agriculture, American farmers, especially in their present distress, feel keenly the hurt of high freight rates, and should be relieved by the immediate correction of the present tariff-a correction that would help everyone and hurt no one.
The statement has often been made in this House-in fact I think it has been made during the present debate and has not been denied-that agriculture in the United States is not prospering. Upon that point I should like to read the following statement from Governor Lowden. taken from the Breeders' Gazette of December 3. 1925:
A Message from Gov. Lowden President of the Holstein-Friesian Association of America
The most hopeful sign for the future of American agriculture is the new interest which other classes are taking in the problem of the farm. It has gradually dawned upon others that the problem of agriculture is

Private Bills
the problem of all. We are beginning to see that in this complex civilization of ours all of the great industries must keep in step. If one lags behind, all the others suffer.
During last summer more than 200 bankers in Nebraska attended the short course in the agricultural college at Lincoln. They returned to their homes enthusiastic, and are preparing to go back another year with the leading farmers of their several communities. The great national organizations of industry are awakening to the fact that the one limiting factor in the future growth of industry is the food supply. They are more and more concerning themselves, therefore, with the well-being of agriculture. I think they begin to see that our greatest asset as a nation is our fertile soil. Whatever depletes that soil must inevitably slow up industry. It is also now recognized by all thoughtful men that an unprofitable agriculture must hasten the exhaustion of the soils. Farmers who are pressed for cash to meet their overhead expenses must devote the largest acreage possible to cash crops, without reference to future productiveness.
Only the other day one of the profundest and wisest students of the agricultural situation of whom I know said to me that the most important thing of all at the present time is to make the country as a whole understand the importance of the farm problem. His idea was that if only all classes of men could be brought to see that there is a farm problem, its correct solution would be seen to be so vastly important to the future of our nation that an answer would be then found.
We can have a balanced nation only if we have a prosperous agriculture. We cannot long have one standard of living in the country and another in town. Those conveniences now regarded as necessities in the city must no-t be considered luxuries upon the farm. We must contrive somehow to improve educational facilities In the country, just as we have improved them in the modern public school in the city. How to balance agriculture economically, socially and educationally with other industries is the problem that confronts us. It is gratifying to know that other forces of society are beginning to recognize the problem.
So the problem in the United States, as in Canada, is how to make agriculture prosper and bring it up to a level with other industries. We in Canada are largely concerned with finding markets, but the most important markets we have to consider are our overseas markets. It is true we have a home market, but without the stabilizing effect of importations coming into the country, that is something not to be depended upon. In the United States the feeling is the same way. Over there the Fordney-McCumber tariff has so reduced importations into the United States that they miss the stabilizing effect of those importations. One hon. member, during the present debate, asked the question why no complaint had ever been voiced by the American people against the Fordney-McCumber tariff. It is not right to say that there has been no complaint against that tariff on the part of the United States people. The research department of the American Farm Bureau Federation, after a thorough investigation, declared that there is practically no benefit to any phase of the American cattle industry from the present tariff,
and that it is a distinct injury to cattle breeders. The United States tariff commission reported to Congress in 1922 that the only effect of the emergency tariff was to injure Canada. In 1923 the American Farm Bureau Federation, the Pennsylvania Farm Bureau, the Illinois Agricultural Association, and others, appealed to the tariff commission for relief from this tariff. Over there they say that the United States tariff on cattle is a direct affront to Canada, which formerly exported some 200.000 head of range cattle annually. It will be seen that a large proportion of the people of the United States do not think very much of the Fordney-McCumber tariff. This article goes on to say:
We make a mockery of our boast that our unguarded Canadian boundary line is imaginary only. We fortified it with worse than guns, "with a tariff of distress and ili will that gave us never a benefit.
Canada errs in attributing this action to the American people. She apparently thinks that our public rules in tariff matters. It is generally expected that in Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime provinces this legislation will not be of very much use, for the simple reason that the people of those provinces can borrow money in eastern Canada just as cheaply as the rates that the western farmers are requesting. A request has been made for longterm credits through federal land banks after

To prove mv contention that one per cent covers the expense of all money in the federal land banks of the United States I will read an advertisement which I tore off the back of the February number of the Geographic Magazine. In regard to the question of conserving our forest resources, those of us who have to travel through those thousand miles of rocky country where we see the marked effects of fire would like to stand behind the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) in everything that his department is doing to conserve the forests of this country.,: Not only is the timber being destroyed in those regions which lie between Ottawa and Winnipeg, but on account of the trees being so near the rock, in fact many of them growing on moss on top of the rock, the moss is burned right off and the rock exposed so that the seed that has been left

The Budget-Mr. Lovie
there is all burned out and the country becomes a barren wilderness instead of being what it should be, one of Canada's assets. The pulpwood industry is certainly one of Canada's assets and if it could be properly looked after, it would for all time bring in good revenues to the Dominion. I am not blaming anyone for the fires that occur there; it is most unfortunate that they should occur, but I should like every Canadian, no matter whether he be Conservative, Liberal or Progressive, to do all in his power to stand behind the Minister of the Interior and any organization who are doing what they can to preserve the wonderful heritage of timber we have in this country. But I am not in favour of preserving this heritage to the extent of advocating an embargo on pulpwood, for the simple reason that eighty per cent of the pulpwood of this country is on crown lands and cannot be exported. Pulpwood taken from those lands must be manufactured in this country. Along the line of the Canadian National railways there are large numbers of settlers who are endeavouring to clean up the land and make it suitable for agriculture. What was solid timberland they are converting into farms, and I for one certainly would not compel those people to take any price offered them for their pulpwood without giving them the benefit of competition. I want to see the Canadian farmer get the best possible price for his timber. I would no more think of putting an embargo on pulpwood obtained from private lands than I would suggest an embargo on wheat; and I know that those of us who come from the west would fight bitterly any proposal to place any such restriction upon the export of wheat. Such a policy is not right and it could never do any good. I do not think it is in the interests of Canada to put an embargo on pulpwood. It is useless to say that the United States need our pulpwood; they do not need our wood, because they have more pulpwood than we have. There is more, timber across the line than there is in Canada. I want to read to the House an advertisement which appears in the Breeder's Gazette of May 6th, 1926, with reference to the timber industry of the United States:
Douglas Fir-America's Permanent Lumber Supply
The densest and heaviest forests the world has ever known stand -to-day between the west slope of the Cascade mountains and the waters of the Pacific.
This forest region contains 26 million acres of towering trees-more than 700 billion feet of merchantable timber-three-quarters of which is Douglas fir; the rest Sitka spruce, western hemlock and western red cedar.
The average yield of these forests is in excess of 30,000 feet per acre and in some cases 150,000 -feet and more. One Douglas fir tree here sometimes produces more lumber than five acres in other forest regions.
What is of more vital interest to the people of the United States is that under modem methods of lumbering, foresting and fire protection, these forests will be a permanent source of lumber supply for the entire country for all time.
Where timber has been cut and fires guarded against countless millions of young Douglas fir trees from nature's own seeding appear and in their vigorous growth offer a new merchantable supply of the finest quality within a comparatively few years.
Emphasizing the importance of Douglas fir, we quote from United States Forest Service Bulletin 88: "Douglas fir iqay, perhaps, be considered the most important of American woods .... Its rapid growth in the Pacific northwest forests, its comparatively wide distribution and the great variety of uses to which it can be put place it first .... As a structural timber it is not surpassed."
We in Canada are just as much interested in preserving our timber supply as the people of the United States are in protecting their resources, although I do not know that we can claim to have gone to the same trouble as they have done to prevent fires. However, I plead with every Canadian to do all that is humanly possible towards preserving this wonderful heritage which we have in this country.

I quote this article in order to make my own reference to the budget as brief and concise as possible. What I am about to read is taken from a Toronto publication which hon. gentlemen who belong to the United Church will recognize. The New Outlook, in its comment on the budget, has this to say:
With the announcement of the tariff changes, and especially the reductions in the income tax the people of Canada got the surprise of their lives. Some modification of the burdens of taxation which have pressed upon all classes since the war were anticipated, but the changes introduced by Hon. James A. Robb, Minister of Finance, in his fourth budget presentation, are so radical as to be almost sensational. A drop from $60 to $10; from $80 to $20; from $100 to $30, etc., on income taxes at one step is something so unusual in budget revisions as to call for universal comment. The reductions in this department' give greater relief to those o-f moderate and small incomes than to those of larger means. The percentage of reduction grows less as the income increases. Few will dispute the fairness of this principle, as by this adjustment the burden of taxation falls on those who are most able to bear it. There is a good deal of dissatisfaction among manufacturing firms, especially motor oar makers and dealers, over the lowering of the tariff on automobiles. This was to be anticipated;

but the closing of factories even for a few days, and the throwing of thousands of men out of work, has not been taken very seriously. A good many have regarded it more as a ,political gesture than as a counsel of necessity. The return to penny postage, and the abolition of the irritating receipt stamp has been hailed with general satisfaction.
