If I may be permitted a personal reference to illustrate the impression which the present prosperous condition in Canada is making upon people in other countries, I may mention the fact that my mother, who is between eighty and ninety years of age, said in a letter I received from her this week that she had been reading everything she could lay her hands on in reference to affairs in Canada, and that she was quite pleased to gather from all that she had read the fact that the country was prosperous and that the outlook was bright as a result of reductions made in this new budget. Obviously, therefore, people outside of Canada are following this budget with interest.
One thing that seems to have been stressed in the debates that have taken place in this House from time to time in connection with the tariff is the desire of some people outside and of some members of parliament to have this country definitely committed to a policy of protection. In this connection, I should like, if the House will bear with me, to read a brief extract from an article discussing the question of protection as a policy for the United States. Certain questions have been asked in that country, and as they are quite applicable to Canada it is well that we should have them answered before we are absolutely committed to the principle of protection. This is the quotation :
Are we to protect ignorance, shiftlessness, incapacity, plants that are out of date, and would be destroyed if not protected or rebuilt? Are we to protect plants that are so badly located or badly managed that the same conditions in a non-protected industry would put them out of business? If we are to do this, then protection becomes an alms-lliouse ^nd asylum for cripples and incompetents, and all such must be protectionists demanding profits and good living by tariff legislation. In fact, protection, honestly considered, can be given only to those industries and persons that are efficient, especially adapted in equipment, location, efficiency and circumstances assuring successful production at as low cost to the consuming public as prevails in non-protected occupations, where the most capable make large profits and .the unfortunate have to quit.
That is:	protection requires the use of every
ordinary advantage in the way of training and efficient persona] capacity, favourable, natural conditions and adequate equipment.

We know that this does not always occur, for there is a good deal of lobbying in and around the House of Commons. Manufacturers, without giving any thought to costs of production, clamour for an increase in the tariff in order to be able to carry on, whereas if they operated under competitive conditions they would be obliged to readjust their affairs or they would probably go out of business altogether. We hear a good deal about closed factories, and the closing of factories is invariably attributed to reductions in the tariff, I do not know whether this is so or not, but I may tell you something. Fiye of us in one day went into southern Ontario and examined the Welland canal from end to end. Returning from Port Colborne we passed a factory with closed doors; I think it was in the town of Thorold. It was a glass factory, and naturally enough we asked why it was closed. The reason given us was that these particular manufacturers could not successfully face the competition they encountered. Several other questions were asked, among them one 'by myself to this effect: "I suppose plenty of sand and other raw materials are available for the manufacture of glass in this locality?" "No," our informant said, "that is one of the unfortunate features of the case. The sand for most of the glass manufactured in this factory had to come from the United States." It seems to me a self-evident fact that factories should be located in close proximity to the source of raw materials, because raw materials cannot be hauled very profitably when the present high cost of transportation is considered. Probably it was just as good that this particular factory went out of existence; all industries khould be so located that they can be carried on economically and profitably. But under the policy of protection industries have grown up without any regard to where the source of raw material was located; the only important point seemed to be that there was sufficient protection to allow them to carry on. I for one *-and I know that the group of whibh I am a member take the same view -wall not stand for the recognition of the principle of protection as the guiding principle of t)he Canadian tariff.

Will the bon. gentleman tell me how close the textile industries in Great Britain are to their supply of raw materials, or the rubber industry in the United States?

The industries referred' to by my hon. friend are a long distance from the source of supply of raw materials, but I would point out that sand is a very heavy commodity, and on that account its transportation is extremely expensive. That is one reason why I emphasize the handicap of carrying on the factory previously referred to.
In conclusion let me say, Mr. Speaker, that when we are asked to commit ourselves definitely to protection the great underlying principle of our tariff it makes me think of some lines of poetry I memorized in my youthful days. We all know that one's memory is more retentive in the days of our youth, and that things learned then remain with us throughout our lives. This particular piece of poetry, committed to memory long since, is is vivid in my mind as when I first learned it. The lines in question run as follows:
And shall the foeman dare, boy,
And shall the foeman dare,
While British hand can wield a brand.
To plant his banner there?
No, by our fathers, no, boy,
No, by our fathers, no!
From England's vales to Scotland's dales Our people thundered "No".
And just as emphatically as those men would have answered, "no" if any foeman dared to lay a hand on that country, I for one will answer "no" in the present crisis in our history; and I will not be a party to committing Canada to the adoption of the policy of protection.

In the few brief remarks I intend to Offer to-night I would like to express my views as a member of the great Canadian family. For I prefer to look upon Canada politically Speaking, as a family. The interests of the family, as a whole, are one, but if any particular member is suffering from peculiar misfortune or disability, special consideration Should be generously extended. If the Maritime provinces, if British Columbia, if the great west, if Ontario and Quebec 'have each peculiar and individual problems, or at times suffer exceptional disadvantage, Jet us not hesitate to give special attention to their condition. Even a gesture makes for goodwill. All this no doubt is subject to the qualification that the concession must not be such as will prove injurious to the family as a whole. Hon. members representing Other sections of the country have placed t'heir positions before the House. I wish to do so, Mr. Speaker, as far as agriculture in the west is concerned. 10 p.m. honest road to Hudson bay and complete , it to tidewater there will be no handicaps at all. The merchant marine will come there and every ship will be needed ; do not sell another boat, because there will be plenty of cargo both ways.
I have taken up a good deal of time on. this matter, but I would have liked to say a great many more things about it. However, there will be another opportunity for me to speak on the Hudson bay project, and for the benefit of the hon. member for Brandon and the hon. member for Lisgar I would like now to give my views on the questions of the tariff and the budget. I am sorry I must.

be absent on Tuesday when the vote is taken, but I have to leave on account of my health; do not think I am shirking my duty. I am going to talk to you now about your pet tariff, and then I will close. I know you want me to come to that soon.
1 know, as do my hon. friends, that the world likes a man who keeps his word. It pays a man to keep his word in western Canada, because half of the business there is conducted by word of mouth. I have seen hundreds of thousands of dollars change hands without the help of our legal friends; they were not needed. They take a man at his word out there, and if you make a statement on any public platform in the west, be sure you are correct; the men there will not stand back of you if you break your word. He formed a tariff board, and immediately emasculated it .

On that account, for the benefit of the hon. member for Brandon and the hon. member for Lisgar I want to put myself on record, so they may go. to Marquette knowing how I stand. I stand for a man who will give his word and keep it. But the Prime Minister went to Kingston on October 21, just before the election, and told the manufacturers there that he believed they should have protection. He remarked:
We realize that our industries here have to have safeguards with respect to competition from other parts of the would; competition from the country to the south of us; competition from conditions as they are in England, and we think that is all the more reason why, in these days of depreciated currency and the like, we should have the benefit of expert advice and information on ail these great questions of the tariff.
The tariff board was formed, and on it was appointed a personal friend of mine, a gentleman I have known for many years, Mr. McKenzie. I know he is not a high tariff man; his father was not and neither is he. The matter of any proposed tariff changes should have been left to that board, in all fairness. The people of western Canada will not take that question as seriously as the hon. member for Lisgar does. He said he was going to watch my step in this House, and that is one of the reasons why I want to place myself on record to-night; I want to show where I stand.
So far as reducing the income tax is concerned, the reduction will help the young man who is getting three or four thousand dollars a year and has some idea of getting married, but it does not help very much the poor fellow who has a little faith in this country and has invested his money in the stocks of Canadian companies. I know a chap who has invested all his life's savings in Canadian companies, to help promote industry in Canada, and who is living on his dividends. Why should you curtail his income? You take mighty good care of your own salaries, and go after the fellow who has a little faith in his country and is drawing an income from dividends from Canadian companies; you tax those dividends three or four times. But you do not tax your 814,000, your $10,000 as ministers, and your $4,000 indemnities. You have that fixed so that you will pay only one tax, but you are going to tax three or four times the dividends of the man who is trying to help build up his country. Think it over. Do not block industry in this country. I am not making this appeal for myself, but for the many people in this country who have their money invested in Canadian companies and are living on their dividends.
The automobile tax reduction is not such a great thing. To me it does not mean very much. I believe in protection, but I do not believe in a manufacturer hiding behind the tariff and making a fortune out of it. As my right hon. leader says, I would see that he was not allowed to do that, especially the man who is manufacturing implements. I would have a tariff board, and I told the people of Marquette that we would have a tariff board. But the kind of tariff board I mean is not one that would take an industry by the scruff of the neck and throw it out of business, saying: Get to one side, you do not know your business. That is what the government has done in connection with this automobile reduction. They have made a drastic cut in the duty. I saw those four

thousand splendid people from Oshawa come and stand in the front of this building. Unlike the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) I did not pick out a young fellow to talk to; I picked out an old fellow, and I asked him, "How long have you lived in Oshawa?" "All my life," he said. "Do you know Mr. McLaughlin?" I asked him. He said "I do." Mr. Speaker, old Mr. McLaughlin had no motor car. I was in California some years ago and bought a motor car there, and I was driving Mr. McLaughlin in my car through the orange groves in that southern country. I drove a McLaughlin buckboard and a McLaughlin buggy on the western prairies, and they were made of real honest material. I bought a car in the United States-get this, Mr. Member from Brandon, and tell the people of Marquette about it; I want you to tell them-I bought a car in the United States, and the spokes flew out of it and the body began to squeak; it was the poorest, shoddiest material that was ever put in a car. I bought a D-45 McLaughlin in Canada; I had it eight years, and I only gave it up because I got so ashamed of the people of Winnipeg asking me, "Mullins, when are you ever going to change that car?" I was afraid to let it go. I would rather have one McLaughlin car made in Canada than twenty shoddy cars made in the United States. Just look at an American Ford coming into the city of Winnipeg. Look at the wheels shimmying and wobbling. I believe the hon. member for Brandon is too shrewd a Scotchman to vote for anything like that. I am sure he would rather give double the money for a Canadian made Ford or a Canadian made McLaughlin. I do not think the hon. member for Brandon had anything to do with this cut in the duty on automobiles. I do not think he wielded the club over the government's head in the matter. I think his sympathies would be with the 4,000 men who came to this parliament asking us to protect their homes and their livelihood.
Some hon. member has said that the city of Hamilton consumes as much beef as we export. I have not checked that up, and I do not know whether it is right or not, but I should like to see a few Hamiltons and Torontos with their industries out west, and I would like to have a few of them scattered through the constituency of Marquette, to consume the products of our great prairies. Would I support a measure that would have a tendency to drive those 4,000 men away from Oshawa where they have made their homes, where they have lived all their lives, where they used to build buggies for Mr. McLaughlin, and where they said they had 
splendid homes and fine working conditions- would I drive them across the line? No, Mr. Speaker, not by my vote in this House, not if I lose my seat in Marquette forty times over; I will never do it. I spoke to these men, and found out from them the inside conditions. I do not hold any brief for Mr. McLaughlin if he was hiding behind the tariff, but I do say that you should have put the tariff board to work and have found out the facts before you touched this industry. It is unfair to cut the tariff without investigation.
Let me say a word to the Labour leaders from Winnipeg. I sat under the ministry of one of them. I listened to him preaching for a number of years, and he was a splendid chap. I do not know what has changed his ideas; I do not know what is the matter with him now. He used to preach splendid sermons in our church.

He has fallen by the
wayside.

I do not know what
has changed him. I do not know anything about his colleague (Mr. Heaps) as a preacher, but I do know about the other man. I know a manufacturer in Winnipeg, manufacturing gloves and mittens. At the request of the industrial bureau I put a little money in that business to help him out. He had a hundred girls at work, and one Saturday he came to me with beads of perspiration standing on his brow, and said he had no money to pay those girls and asked me to help him out. He took me over to the Bank of Toronto and got me to endorse a paper for him so that those girls could receive their weekly pay. That fellow was not drawing as big a salary from the business as those girls were. They were making from $25 to $28 a week, and that poor fellow who was manufacturing these gloves only drew $100 a month. As I walked across the market square with him I heard a man standing on a soap box fairly eating up the poor employer; he was just devouring him, running #ie poor employer down, and here was a poor employer with me who was sweating drops of blood to meet the pay cheques on Saturday night. So I say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, have a kindly word for the manufacturers. They are not all you think of them; be fair to them. I say that honest labour has a right to organize, and to strike if they are being oppressed by capital-yes, every time; but do not be unfair to the manufacturer. These men who oame from Oshawa were being treated fairly. Every one of them that

I talked to spoke very highly of his employer, and they were all well satisfied with their working conditions.
I am going to support the amendment, and I want to let the people in Marquette know that the government did not carry out its promise that it would appoint a tariff board and have a thorough inquiry into the question of the tariff before taking action. Mr. Speaker, when at the opening of this session, the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) proposed your reelection as Speaker, I enthusiastically approved of it like every other member of the House. Of course, you were best qualified to hold that position under the abnormal and difficult conditions due to the result of the last general election. But in doing so, the Liberal party gave the country and parliament further evidence of their self-denial and they deprived themselves of the services of one of the most Able members of parliament and of the most eloquent orators of our race. Mr. Speaker, let the first words that I utter in this chamber be words of hearty congratulation to you.
I do not intend to speak very long on the subject which is now before the House, but I would not take up the budget at once without saying to the hon. member for Toronto Northeast (Mr. Baker), like hon. members who preceded me, how much we appreciated his delicate feelings in expressing himself in this House in the French language. The example which he set is worth being followed by every one of his English speaking colleagues. The compliment which he paid to us was appreciated not only in this House, but I venture to say in our whole province and the people of my district whom I met on my last week-end trip have asked me to thank the hon. member for Toronto Northeast on their behalf and to tell him that if he keeps on studying the French language, they will soon be glad to call him " Boulanger " and should he go further, to open to him the

doors of the Liberal party. The electors of the constituency which I have the honour to represent have received with a great deal of pleasure, I should say with enthusiasm, the budget as presented by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). I come from a district where wealthy people are an exception. A good number of my constituents, perhaps not the average but those who have some means, enjoy a decent comfort. They were among those who, under the old scale of taxation had to pay an income tax ranging from $40 to $200 a year. The present budget decreases their charges considerably and enables them to get a little more than what they formerly used to consider as luxury; it enables them to give their children a better education and, at the same time, to enjoy more of the pleasures of life. They have been just as happy to hear that the Minister of Finance did not have to show deficits or to announce an increase of the debt. Judging from the present budget, we may state that our country has gone through the after-war crisis and that, in the future, our financial results will favourably compare with those obtained by our beloved chieftain, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Ever since the beginning of this session the members sitting to your left strove to show, in all possible manners, why and how they have been reelected as members of this House. They state that, in their constituencies, the only important issue was that of high protection. Since this session began hon. members from the Maritime provinces have told us that they had been elected, not only in order to favour protection, but in order to uphold the rights of those provinces. The members from the West told us: We must have freight rates which will enable us to ship our products to the European markets; but everyone of them favours protection. Among the members who sit to your left, Mr. Speaker, I seek in vain for one who said: I favour high protection, I want a higher tariff on such and such an article manufactured in this country; I would like to see the duty raised 10 or 20 per cent above what it is to-day. They are in a general way in favour of high protection, and nothing more.
With us, Mr. Speaker, conditions differ somewhat from those in the rest of the country. In the province of Quebec, the people are not exclusively supporters of free trade, but they do not advocate a high tariff, and you will readily understand why. In such constituencies as are depending on industry, it is more than likely that the voters should demand more protection in favour of the
The Budget-Mr. Dussault

industries on which they depend for their living; but when hon. gentlemen on the opposition side tell us that the province of Quebec as a whole is advocating protection, I feel that it is my duty to take exception to such a statement. For instance, Mr. Speaker, in the constituency of Levis, which I have the honour to represent in this House, there is not a single industry that is dissatisfied with the extent of protection enjoyed at the present time; and for years and years back, the people of Levis have been taxed for the benefit of the manufacturers. For that reason, it would hardly be fitting to come and tell them: You ought to consider yourselves fortunate in having to pay a higher price for anything you purchase inasmuch as what you thus pay goes towards the making up of wages earned by your workers! There is no worker in our district who can make a living out of the wages resulting from a high tariff policy. Should the big interests ever decide to establish any new industry in the city of Levis or in the town of Lauzon, I think that my constituents would be justified in protecting and doing their utmost towards safeguarding the capital from which they would derive their means of subsistence. But until such industries are established I see no reason why our people should be keen on paying a much higher price for anything from which they derive no benefit, directly or indirectly. And, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the people in Ontario are beginning to admit the fitness of what I have just said. In fact, last night I clipped from the Star a short item reproduced from the Hamilton Spectator:
Everything that gives Quebec and Ontario a common aim, everything that turns the sympathetic attention of men in Ontario to Quebec and of men in Quebec to Ontario, is of value to both. The growth of manufactures in Quebec will in time bring industrialist and workman there to see the viewpoint of the Ontario manufacturer.
That, Mr. Speaker, is exactly what we said to the voters during the last electoral campaign. We said: "If the manufacturers expect the province of Quebec to patronize them, the least they can do is to come along and let us benefit by their investments and thus assist in the development of our province."
The chief industry in my constituency is that of steel shipbuilding and neither the employers nor the workers engaged in that industry could depend on protection for the betterment of the conditions they are confronted with; a high tariff would solve none of their problems. Their competitors in that branch of business are British firms, from the United Kingdom, and every one knows that

no party would ever undertake to increase the tariff to the detriment of British shipbuilders. The remedy to the ills suffered by our workingmen employed in that particular industry is within reach of the administrators of this country: it is the readjustment of dry dock charges for ships in need of repairs, and such a readjustment can be made without any loss of revenue to the public treasury. Rates charged for the use of the dry dock in the case of ships to undergo permanent repairs should be decreased by half, so as to enable our Canadian shipyards to compete successfully with foreign shipbuilders.
This, as a rule, is what takes place when a large ship, liner or cargo boat is stranded somewhere in the river-the insurance companies concerned in the salvage of that ship immediately call for tenders from the different Canadian shipbuilding companies as well as from American and English shipyards. When thus competing, Canadian builders, as for instance those of Levis, must add to the cost of actual repairs such rates as they are compelled to pay for the use of the docks. Their competitors in England, who have been engaged in that industry for centuries, own their own dry docks and, in the price of their tenders do not include docking charges. Mr. Speaker, here in Canada, the department of Public Works would only have to lower by one half their docking charges and as an immediate result, our Canadian shipbuilders would be in a position to compete with the British shipyards. In fact, what happens when the Canadian employer is thus prevented from securing a contract? The ship is raised and laid up in the dry docks where she undergoes temporary repairs, which means, for instance, that whatever plates of the hull are warped or twisted are not even removed but covered with new ones; then the ship is launched again and with a full or half cargo, proceeds to Europe where the permanent repairs are to be made. If dry dbck charges allowed our contractors to compete for the job not only would it not cost one cent more to the country, but the vessel remaining here for a full month would be a four or five times better paying proposition than when the length of its stay is a mere three days; moreover, our workers would find employment for one, two or three months. You are aware, Mr. Speaker, that common interest demands that those engaged in ship construction and repairs should live near the dry dock, since a dry dock without expert workmen would be like a hospital without a doctor; if these men are not kept employed they must

The Budget-Mr. Dussault
look for work elsewhere. I do not say they will leave the country but they will go away in search of a living. It is one of navigation's essential needs, Mr. Speaker, that dry docks be properly supplied with material and labour.
But there is more than that. The other day when we were discussing the estimates of the Marine department, on an item of $35,000 being called, an item having to do with continuing the subsidies paid for salvaging equipment in the province of Quebec and in British Columbia, some hon. mem|bers asked the Minister of Marine what services had been rendered to navigation by the Quebec Salvage and Wrecking Co., which receives an annual grant of $25,000 from the Dominion government. Since nearly all the employees of this company come from my riding, and since the main artery of the company's operations is in the city of Levis, on the south side of Quebec harbour, I know better than any other what signal service these people have rendered navigation along the entire course off the St. Lawrence. This company, which employs all the men I have just mentioned, has a very powerful equipment; I even venture to state that no other firm of the same character in the whole of the Dominion, on either the Atlantic or the Pacific coast, can compare with it in this respect. In order to keep this entire outfit under steam during the season of navigation, to be ready to respond instantly to a call for succour, to keep and pay regularly skilled salvage workers, the company is put to an expense far beyond its income; hence it would naturally operate at a heavy loss. It was to avoid this loss that the Marine department was asked to grant a subsidy. To show how well this company does its work I shall cite one instance which occurred in our district last December. On December 6th the steamer Airedale started down the river from Montreal; at Ile-aux-Coudres, just below Quebec, she ran ashore going at full speed. The underwriters got into touch immediately with the Quebec Salvage and Wrecking Co., and the latter lost no time in desp>aitching a wrecking crew to the scene. But the company's equipment was not powerful enough for the work in hand; they had to call on the Marine department for help with boats and men. In passing I wish to congratulate the Minister of Marine on the fine work done by his department at the time. Mr. Speaker, in cold December weather when ice was beginning to form on the river these men succeeded in floating the vessel in four days: they started on December 10th; on December 15th the Airedale had been floated, brought
to Quebec and put in dry dock. On December 17th, two days later, she left Quebec, reloaded with all her cargo. You readily grasp, Mr. Speaker, the importance to navigation of such assistance to ships in distress. You know that on the 1st of November each year, because of the approach of winter, the shipping underwriters charge a special rate not on vessels alone but on their cargoes as well. If, on account of neglect on the part of the government or shortsightedness in the Marine department, this ship had not been salvaged the insurance companies would have been obliged to pay the full value of the policies on the boat, which amounted to a considerable sum, and on the cargo besides. The insurance companies would have passed these charges along to alM the goods shipped and all the boats leaving Quebec or the St. Lawrence after December, and the following year insurance rates would have been raised; and when an insurance company has once raised its rates you know what trouble it is to have rates reduced later to the old figure. As you can see by what happened in this particular instance, dry o'ocks, salvage equipment, skilled labour, the Marine department, the lighting of the channel, the buoy service, dredging by the department of Public Works or of Marine, aill form part of the one scheme of things, all have a share in making the St. Lawrence an inland waterway renowned for its safety in shipping circles the world over. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that next year the Minister of Marine will not be bothered so much when he asks for a renewal of this subsidy.
Increasing the safety of navigation on the St. Lawrence will do no harm to traffic on the lakes. If the insurance companies raise their rates on the St. Lawrence shippers in Quebec province will not be the only ones to suffer; the same higher rates will be levied on goods coming from Ontario via the lakes and on goods from the west. So when these gentlemen help to keep the St. Lawrence salvage service well equipped they are striving, like the rest of the country, to ensure favourable rates.
Mr. Speaker, among all the members from the Maritime provinces who have told the House of the evils that beset that part of the country only one pointed to any remedy. I am speaking of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley). After explaining in detail just what industries are affected in his province, after an eloquent plea for his fellow-citizens, he indicated as a remedy the reestablishment at Moncton of the administration of the Intercolonial with the understanding that the railway would be maintained and operated in the interest of the Maritime prov-
The Budget-Mr, Dussault

inces and under the direction of high officials from those provinces, and he said: "That is what I demand, and what I will continue to demand as long as I sit in this House."
Well, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's stand appears rather selfish to me. Of course the Intercolonial serves the Maritime provinces, but it also serves all the counties on the south shore from Montreal to Campbellton; and if there be two paying divisions on this railroad they are certainly those between Montreal and Levis and Levis and Campbellton. It is only in Quebec province that the railroad makes any profit at all; and I do not think it quite fair that the system should be operated solely for and by the Maritime provinces when it derives its revenue from the population of our province. Why is such a request made? The reason is not far to seek; certain members are evidently dissatisfied with the way patronage is exercised in their district. And I can quote the hon. member for Kings (Mr. J. A. Macdonald) who said that in his part of the country the only people employed are those recommended by the Liberal committee or the Liberal member, or ex-member, or the Liberal candidate. It is a pity the hon. gentleman doesn't come and see how things are where I come from; if he thinks he is on a red-hot gridiron he would find that I am not on a bed of roses. There things are just the opposite: patronage is in the hands of the Conservatives and is used for the sole advantage of Conservatives. Since October 29 last I have recommended people three or four times, not because they were Liberals but because they really were in need of earning the money; I would no sooner recommend a man than he would be discharged forthwith. So I wonder what it would profit these people from the Maritime provinces to do away with the staunch friends they have just now in the head offices of the railway. And since that is the way with patronage, Mr. Speaker, I wish you would come down to my riding and see some of the properties belonging to the Railway department. You would find a deep-sea wharf built by the Department of Public Works and later given over to the Intercolonial. I am certain that not $1,000 a year has been spent for the maintenance of this wharf, and if repairs are not undertaken immediately it will be carried away by the ice. You will say: But you should take the matter up with the railway board. The railway commissioners tell us:	We cannot pay attention to the claims of members of parliament, particularly Liberal members:	that
would be patronage.

I do not see why we should not bring about a better understanding between the people of the Maritime provinces and the people of the province of Quebec. We are all anxious to ensure their full rights to these provinces; however, they should not tiy to trespass on the rights of their neighbours. I would be perfectly willing to have an Intercolonial Commission composed of representatives of the Maritimes and of one or two representatives from Quebec province in the interest of the south shore of the St. Lawrence from Montreal to Campbellton. But when it is suggested to establish one sole dictator at Moncton and to operate the Intercolonial for the exclusive benefit of the Maritime provinces, we claim that nothing of the sort was promised at the time of Confederation.
Nevertheless, I wish to congratulate the hon. member from Pictou (Mr. Cantley) on having had the courage-lacking in his colleagues from the Maritimes-to tell us frankly what he is after and what his constituents expect. We know that these gentlemen want the railroad administered for themselves and only by their own people, without consulting the other provinces. Not a very auspicious start, I'll admit, for negotiating an agreement between the Maritimes and Quebec, where the Intercolonial passes; but it is a start at any rate. However, Mr. Speaker, let me say that we of the province of Quebec will not allow ourselves-and our constituents would not stand for it if we were to countenance such a proceeding-to be swept aside in the administration of a public service which is absolutely essential to our trade. Mark you, I am not speaking of secession. During the election, last October, there was some mention made of secession in the Maritime provinces; this was badly received in Quebec. As a new member in this House I found that the following which appeared in the Halifax Herald of February 18th last was in very bad taste:
The possibilities of commencing a secession movement in the Maritime provinces were to-day informally discussed by a handful of local businessmen, headed hy Walter H. Termant, a prominent manufacturer of this town. It was stated that a meeting to formally debate the topic would be called at an early date and Mr. Tennant was authorized to secure a speaker and arrange the details of the meeting.
Mr. Speaker, you know that during the period when the province of Quebec had most reason to complain of the treatment we received at the hands of those who governed us, nobody ever raised these cries of secession, because they were known to be too dangerous. If to-day it is sought to create a movement

The Budget-Mr. Charters
along that line in the rest of the country and bring about a political divorce you can rest assured that Quebec will be against the divorce no matter what form it may take. Quebec will be the last province to separate from her sister provinces; but she will know how to safeguard her rights in their entirety, no matter what may happen.

Mr. Speaker, at this stage of the debate and at this hour of the night I have no intention of delaying the House for more than a few minutes, and 1 rise only for the purpose of making an observation or two regarding matters directly affecting the people of the district from which I come. The greater number of the people in the county of Peel are engaged in what is called mixed farming in the widest sense of the term, in stock raising, grain growing, dairying, fruit and1 vegetable growing and other lines akin thereto. Others in the urban section are employed in the manufacture of 'boots and shoes, woollens, bricks and the growling of flowers.
These industries and occupations are all dependent for success on the home market, something that we hear very little about during 'this debate in comparison with other years. The value of the home market is well illustrated by three or four items which I wish to present. In one year, 1922, of all the food produced in the Dominion of Canada the following are the percentages consumed by the Canadian people:

Other lines of vegetables, fruit and so on were consumed in the same proportions. The portion of the home market with which the people I represent are most directly concerned is that which consists of the cities of Toronto, Hamilton and all the adjacent towns and villages. Within a radius of forty-five to fifty miles there is an urban population of no leiss than 700,000 people, a population greater than that of Alberta, or Manitoba, or Nova Scotia, and almost equal to that of Saskatchewan, a population comprising one-twelfth of all the people of Canada. A district of that size surely deserves the consideration of the government and of tmembrs of parliament generally. In, that area there are manufacturers of all kinds whose wants have to be supplied. They are supplied' by the farmers of the surrounding districts. Any policy that
retards progress in that section, that fails tc promote prosperity in that urban district, injures very greatly the farmers of the surrounding country. It is contended, and no! without a good deal of justification, that everj one of the industries and occupations to which I have referred are injured to some extent because of the action or on account of the inaction of the present administration. For that reason there is no free trade sentiment in the county of Peel or the adjoining counties of Halton, Lincoln, Wellington and York or indeed from Kingston down to Niagara Falls, and there has been no free trade sentiment in my constituency for a number of years.
In the election of 1921 the opponents of the then government took the ground that the tariff was no longer an issue and that nothing was to be gained by discussing it. In the election contest of October last the candidate supporting the administration took exactly the same ground, stating not that the tariff was too high, but that in many cases it was much too low. I want to refer to one or two of his statements. Speaking at Erindale, where hon. members will probably recall the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made the second speech in the campaign, the candidate supporting the present administration made this reference to the tariff:
The whole tariff on 'fruits and vegetables is absurd under present conditions, and if I am Elected to parliament, I shall make every effort to secure the adjustment to prevent the flooding of our market with produce from the southern states at the same season when it is in direct competition with our own home-grown stuff.
Again speaking at Brampton on October 27 he said:
